families.source: UKHSA mpox vaccination information for healthcare practitioners
families.topic: routine mpox vaccination eligibility, MVA-BN products, dosing, administration and programme delivery
families.page_title: Mpox vaccination: information for healthcare practitioners
evidence_points: The guidance supports delivery of the routine mpox vaccination programme in England.
The routine programme targets people at higher ongoing risk of exposure under programme eligibility criteria.
MVA-BN vaccine is used to protect against mpox infection and severe disease.
The programme is distinct from outbreak-response and occupational-health vaccination pathways.
The guidance addresses subcutaneous and intradermal administration.
It covers dose intervals and co-administration with other vaccines.
It includes considerations for people under 18 years of age.
It describes management of vaccine errors and special situations.
Eligibility cannot be inferred from sexual orientation alone without applying the programme criteria.
Vaccination decisions require the correct programme pathway, risk assessment, age, immune status and dose history.

families.source: UKHSA mpox vaccination resources for contacts
families.topic: post-exposure mpox vaccination information, eligibility, consent and family advice
evidence_points: The resources are for people offered vaccination after contact with an mpox case.
They include information for families and other eligible contacts.
The MVA vaccine is used to reduce the risk or severity of mpox.
Vaccination is offered only to contacts who meet the relevant eligibility assessment.
A single dose may be offered promptly after exposure in specified circumstances.
Post-exposure timing affects the expected preventive benefit.
Consent information is included for the vaccination pathway.
Vaccination does not remove the need to monitor for symptoms and follow contact advice.
Being named as a contact does not automatically establish eligibility for vaccination.
Eligibility requires contact categorisation, timing, previous doses, contraindications and public-health advice.

families.source: UKHSA guidance for managing close community contacts of invasive group A streptococcal disease
families.topic: iGAS household, childcare and care-home contact risk assessment, chemoprophylaxis and surveillance
families.page_title: Invasive group A streptococcal disease: managing close contacts in community settings
evidence_points: The guidance supports management of close community contacts of probable or confirmed iGAS cases.
It includes pathways for household-type, childcare and care-home settings.
Local microbiology laboratories should retain relevant isolates and refer them when required.
Health protection teams should be notified urgently about iGAS cases.
Contact definitions and action use the diagnosis date and specified exposure windows.
Selected close contacts may be offered antibiotic chemoprophylaxis.
Contacts are monitored for compatible symptoms during a defined surveillance period.
Care-home cases require assessment for possible acquisition and linked cases.
Being present in the same institution does not automatically make every person a close contact.
Action requires diagnosis, setting, contact intensity, timing, vulnerability and epidemiological linkage.

families.topic: stepwise iGAS contact and outbreak management for households, childcare and care homes
families.page_title: Accessible text versions of the 4 algorithms
evidence_points: The publication provides accessible text versions of four iGAS management algorithms.
Algorithm 1 covers a case in a household-type setting.
Algorithm 2 covers a case linked to a nursery, school or childcare setting.
Algorithm 3 covers a single iGAS case in a care home.
Algorithm 4 covers a suspected or confirmed iGAS outbreak in a care home.
The algorithms include urgent notification and microbiology actions.
Care-home assessment includes layout, staffing, resident links and previous cases.
Suspected outbreaks can require an outbreak control team and reference-laboratory support.
Two cases are not automatically linked without person, place, timing or microbiological evidence.
The algorithms supplement rather than replace the complete national iGAS guidance and professional judgement.
